title: Central tendency and dispersion
summary: The [[mean|mean]], [[median|median]] and mode describe the centre of a data set; the IQR and [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] describe its spread. You find them with your GDC, estimate the mean of grouped data, and see what shifting or scaling the data does.

goals.text: Find the mean, median and mode of a list or frequency table, and the mean both by formula and with your GDC.
Estimate the mean of grouped data from mid-interval values, and find the [[modal-class|modal class]].
Find [[quartile|quartiles]] and the IQR with your GDC, and explain why a by-hand quartile can differ.
Find the standard deviation and [[variance|variance]] with your GDC, and interpret them in context.
Say how adding to or multiplying every value changes the mean and standard deviation.

synonyms: effect of adding a constant on mean and standard deviation

before.hint: Substitute $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$ and add the four terms.

before.prompt: A reservoir holds $2648.7$ megalitres. Round this to 3 [[significant-figures|significant figures]].
before.hint: Count from the first non-zero digit, then look at the next digit.
before.explain: The 3rd figure is $4$ and the next digit is $8$, so round up: $2650$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.6}}.

before.prompt: Lap times, $t$ seconds, are grouped as $40 \le t < 45$, $45 \le t < 50$ and $50 \le t < 55$. Which class holds a time of exactly $45$ seconds?
before.hint: Which class includes its left end?
before.explain: $45 \le t < 50$ includes $45$; $40 \le t < 45$ stops just below it. Revise it in {{lesson:4.2}}.

blocks.text: A podcast's last $8$ episodes lasted $42, 37, 51, 37, 45, 40, 37, 47$ minutes. How long is a typical episode? Three different averages answer that.

blocks.statement: The [[mean|mean]] of $n$ values is their total divided by $n$: $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$. In this [[sigma-notation|sigma notation]], $\sum x$ means the sum of all the values.
blocks.plain: Share the total out equally between the values.

blocks.statement: The [[median|median]] is the middle value when the data are in order: the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value. When $n$ is even, it is the mean of the two middle values.
blocks.plain: At least half the data lie at or below it, and at least half at or above it.

blocks.statement: The mode is the value that occurs most often. A data set can have more than one mode, or none.

blocks.question: The lengths, in minutes, of $8$ podcast episodes are $42, 37, 51, 37, 45, 40, 37, 47$. Find the mean, median and mode, and comment on which best describes a typical episode.
steps: Mean: the total is $336$ and $n = 8$, so $\bar{x} = \frac{336}{8} = 42$ minutes.
Median: in order, $37, 37, 37, 40, 42, 45, 47, 51$. With $n = 8$, average the $4$th and $5$th values: $\frac{40 + 42}{2} = 41$ minutes.
Mode: $37$ appears three times, more than any other length.
Comment: the mean and median are close, so either describes a typical episode. The mode, $37$, is the shortest length, so it doesn't.

blocks.text: In a frequency table, each value $x_{i}$ occurs $f_{i}$ times, so it adds $f_{i}x_{i}$ to the total. This formula is in the booklet.
Here $k$ is the number of different values, and $n$ is the total frequency, not the number of columns.

blocks.question: A hotel records how many nights, $x$, each of $60$ guests stayed. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline f & 18 & 15 & 12 & 9 & 6 \end{array}$ (a) Find the mean by the formula, and check it with your GDC. (b) Find the median and the mode.
steps: On the GDC, enter the values $1$ to $5$ in one list and the frequencies in another, then run one-variable statistics. Check $n = 60$, then read $\bar{x} = 2.5$.
(b) With $n = 60$, the median is the mean of the $30$th and $31$st values. The first $18$ guests stayed $1$ night, and guests $19$ to $33$ stayed $2$, so both are $2$.
The median is $2$ nights. The mode is $1$ night, the value with the highest frequency, $18$.
The mean is above the median because a few long stays pull it up.

blocks.text: Taking the middle column of a frequency table, here $x = 3$, as the median. Count through the frequencies to the middle data value.

blocks.prompt: A tram was late by $3, 11, 6, 8, 14, 5$ minutes on six days. Find the median delay.
blocks.hint: Put the values in order first. There is an even number of them.
blocks.explain: In order: $3, 5, 6, 8, 11, 14$. The middle two are $6$ and $8$, so the median is $7$ minutes.

blocks.prompt: Find the mean number of siblings, $x$, of these $25$ students. $\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline f & 6 & 8 & 5 & 4 & 2 \end{array}$
blocks.hint: Find $\sum f_{i}x_{i}$, then divide by the total frequency.
blocks.explain: $\sum f_{i}x_{i} = 0 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 8 = 38$ and $n = 25$, so $\bar{x} = 1.52$. Dividing $38$ by the $5$ columns gives $7.6$, which is wrong.

blocks.prompt: Lena's first $6$ runs this month have a mean of $5.5$ km. After her $7$th run, the mean of all seven is $6$ km. How far was her $7$th run, in km?
blocks.hint: Turn each mean into a total, using total $= n \times \bar{x}$.
blocks.explain: The totals are $7 \times 6 = 42$ km and $6 \times 5.5 = 33$ km, so the $7$th run was $42 - 33 = 9$ km.

sections.heading: Grouped data: estimated mean and modal class

blocks.text: Sometimes you only know which [[class-interval|class interval]] each value lies in. Then you can only estimate the mean.
Treat every value in a class as if it sat at the class's mid-interval value: $\frac{a + b}{2}$ for the class $a \le x < b$.
Use the booklet formula with these as the $x_{i}$. The result is an estimate, because the actual values are unknown.

blocks.statement: For grouped data with equal class widths, the [[modal-class|modal class]] is the class with the highest frequency.

blocks.question: A bank timed how long, $t$ minutes, $40$ customers waited. $\begin{array}{c|c} t & f \\ \hline 0 \le t < 5 & 7 \\ 5 \le t < 10 & 14 \\ 10 \le t < 15 & 11 \\ 15 \le t < 20 & 6 \\ 20 \le t < 25 & 2 \end{array}$ (a) Write down the modal class. (b) Find an estimate of the mean waiting time. (c) Explain why your answer to (b) is an estimate.
steps: (a) The classes all have width $5$, and the highest frequency is $14$. So the modal class is $5 \le t < 10$.
(b) The mid-interval values are $2.5, 7.5, 12.5, 17.5, 22.5$.
$\sum f_{i}x_{i} = 7 \times 2.5 + 14 \times 7.5 + 11 \times 12.5 + 6 \times 17.5 + 2 \times 22.5 = 410$, so the estimate is $\frac{410}{40} = 10.25$ minutes.
(c) Only the class of each wait is known, so each wait is replaced by the middle of its class.

blocks.text: Using a class boundary, such as $5$ or $10$, as the value for a class. Use the mid-interval value, here $7.5$.

blocks.question: The heights, $h$ cm, of $90$ sunflowers in a trial field are shown. $\begin{array}{c|c} h & f \\ \hline 100 \le h < 120 & 6 \\ 120 \le h < 140 & 15 \\ 140 \le h < 160 & 28 \\ 160 \le h < 180 & 25 \\ 180 \le h < 200 & 16 \end{array}$ Use your calculator to find an estimate of the mean height. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Write down the lists you enter: mid-interval values $110, 130, 150, 170, 190$ and frequencies $6, 15, 28, 25, 16$. That line earns the method mark.
Run one-variable statistics with the frequency list attached. Check that $n = 90$: if it shows $5$, the frequencies are missing.
Read $\bar{x} = 156.666\ldots$, and round only now: about $157$ cm.
Interpret: the mean height of the sunflowers in the trial is estimated at about $157$ cm, inside the modal class, $140 \le h < 160$.

blocks.prompt: The distances, $d$ km, cycled by $25$ commuters are grouped as $0 \le d < 6$: $7$; $6 \le d < 12$: $10$; $12 \le d < 18$: $8$. Find an estimate of the mean distance, to 3 s.f.
What is the modal class of these puzzle times, $t$ seconds? $\begin{array}{c|c} t & f \\ \hline 20 \le t < 30 & 8 \\ 30 \le t < 40 & 14 \\ 40 \le t < 50 & 11 \\ 50 \le t < 60 & 7 \end{array}$
blocks.hint: The answer is a class, not a single number.
blocks.explain: The highest frequency, $14$, is in $30 \le t < 40$. The modal class depends on frequency, not on how large the values are. Give the class, not the frequency $14$ or the mid-interval value $35$.

blocks.text: A measure of dispersion says how spread out the data are. The [[range-of-a-data-set|range]] is the simplest, but one extreme value can change it a lot.

The [[quartile|quartiles]] cut the ordered data into four roughly equal parts: about a quarter of the values lie below the lower quartile $Q_{1}$, and about three quarters below the upper quartile $Q_{3}$.
1. To find the quartiles by hand, put the data in order and find the median.
2. Split the data into a lower half and an upper half. When $n$ is odd, leave the median out of both halves.
3. $Q_{1}$ is the median of the lower half, and $Q_{3}$ is the median of the upper half.
The [[interquartile-range|interquartile range]] (IQR) is the spread of the middle half of the data, so a few extreme values have little effect on it.

blocks.question: Eleven students held a plank for as long as they could. Their times, in seconds, were $58, 73, 96, 64, 112, 81, 104, 69, 91, 107, 86$. (a) Find $Q_{1}$, $Q_{3}$ and the IQR. (b) Another student keeps the median in both halves. What IQR does she get?
steps: (a) In order: $58, 64, 69, 73, 81, 86, 91, 96, 104, 107, 112$. The median is the $6$th value, $86$; leave it out of both halves.
$\mathrm{IQR} = 104 - 69 = 35$ seconds.
(b) Keeping $86$, the halves have $6$ values each: $Q_{1} = \frac{69 + 73}{2} = 71$ and $Q_{3} = \frac{96 + 104}{2} = 100$, so her IQR is $29$ seconds.
Both are correct for their method. Your GDC uses the method in (a).

blocks.text: Several methods for quartiles are in use, so a by-hand quartile and a technology quartile can differ slightly. Each is right for its method.
In the exam, find quartiles of [[discrete-data|discrete data]] with your GDC. In their usual settings, the three models in these notes leave the median out when $n$ is odd, as in (a).

blocks.question: The numbers of books, $x$, that $45$ students read last month are shown. $\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline f & 5 & 9 & 11 & 8 & 6 & 4 & 2 \end{array}$ (a) Use your calculator to find $Q_{1}$, $Q_{3}$ and the IQR. (b) Interpret the IQR.
steps: (a) Enter $0$ to $6$ in one list and the frequencies in another. Run one-variable statistics and check that $n = 45$.
Scroll down to read $Q_{1} = 1$ and $Q_{3} = 4$, so $\mathrm{IQR} = 4 - 1 = 3$ books.
Check by counting: the lower half is the first $22$ values, and its $11$th and $12$th values are both $1$.
(b) The middle half of the students read between $1$ and $4$ books: a spread of $3$ books.

blocks.text: Giving the range when asked for the IQR. Subtract the quartiles, not the smallest value from the largest.

blocks.prompt: Eight friends took $11, 19, 23, 26, 28, 33, 38, 44$ minutes to walk to school. Work out the interquartile range of these times, in minutes.
blocks.hint: Each half has $4$ values. Find the median of each half.

blocks.prompt: Seven parcels weigh $3, 6, 8, 10, 15, 21, 24$ kg. Omar works out $Q_{1}$ by hand, keeping the median in both halves, and gets $7$ kg. His GDC gives $Q_{1} = 6$ kg. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: Find the lower half twice: once with the median $10$, once without.

options.text: The GDC is wrong, so Q1 is 7
Omar made an arithmetic slip, so Q1 is 6
They use different methods, and each value is right for its method

blocks.explain: With the median, the lower half is $3, 6, 8, 10$, so $Q_{1} = 7$. Without it, the lower half is $3, 6, 8$, so $Q_{1} = 6$. Both methods are in use.

verify.truth: They use different methods, and each value is right for its method

blocks.text: The IQR uses only the quartiles. The standard deviation uses every value: it measures how far the values typically lie from the mean.

blocks.alt: Two dot plots on one temperature scale from 20 to 40 degrees Celsius. City A has five dots close together at 27, 29, 30, 31 and 33. City B has five dots spread out at 21, 24, 30, 36 and 39. A dashed line marks the mean, 30, of both cities.
blocks.caption: Both cities have mean $30$ °C. City B's temperatures lie further from the mean, so its standard deviation is larger.

blocks.statement: The [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]] $\sigma$ measures the typical distance of the data values from the mean. The [[variance|variance]] is its square, $\sigma^{2}$.
blocks.plain: A small standard deviation means the values sit close to the mean.

blocks.text: In the exam you find $\sigma$ with your GDC only. One small case by hand shows what it measures: the variance is the mean squared distance from the mean, $\sigma^{2} = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2}}{n}$.

blocks.question: Kai slept $6, 8, 7, 9, 5$ hours on five nights. Find the variance and standard deviation by hand.
steps: Mean: $\bar{x} = \frac{35}{5} = 7$ hours.
Distances from the mean: $-1, 1, 0, 2, -2$. They add up to $0$, so square them first.
$\sigma = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\ldots \approx 1.41$ hours: a typical night is about $1.4$ hours from the mean.

blocks.text: Your GDC shows two standard deviations. For the standard deviation of a data set, use $\sigma_{x}$, which divides by $n$ as above. Ignore $s_{x}$ (or $S_{x}$), which divides by $n - 1$.
At HL, $s_{n-1}^{2}$, which divides by $n - 1$, is used as an unbiased estimate of a population's variance from a sample.

blocks.question: Eight friends' times, in minutes, for a charity fun run were $36, 44, 28, 40, 47, 33, 38, 42$. Use your calculator to find (a) the mean, (b) the standard deviation and (c) the variance of the times. (d) Interpret the standard deviation.
steps: Enter the times in a list and run one-variable statistics. Check that $n = 8$.
(a) $\bar{x} = 38.5$ minutes.
(b) $\sigma_{x} = 5.744\ldots$, so $\sigma \approx 5.74$ minutes. Keep the full value for (c).
(c) $\sigma^{2} = (5.744\ldots)^{2} = 33$ minutes². Squaring the rounded $5.74$ would give $32.9$ instead.
(d) The friends' times typically lie about $5.7$ minutes from the mean of $38.5$ minutes.

blocks.text: Quoting $s_{x}$ from the GDC. The standard deviation of a data set is $\sigma_{x}$; mark schemes usually give no accuracy mark for $s_{x}$, which is for an unbiased estimate of a population (HL).

blocks.prompt: A gardener measures the $4$ leaves on a seedling: $4, 7, 9, 12$ cm. Find the standard deviation of the leaf lengths with your GDC.
blocks.hint: Use the GDC value that divides by $n$.
blocks.explain: $\sigma_{x} = 2.915\ldots \approx 2.92$. The value $3.37$ is $s_{x}$, and $8.5$ is the variance.

blocks.prompt: Use your calculator to estimate the standard deviation of the $90$ sunflower heights from the grouped data section, to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: Enter the mid-interval values with their frequencies, then read $\sigma_{x}$.
blocks.explain: $\sigma_{x} = 22.90\ldots \approx 22.9$ cm. Like the mean, it is only an estimate.

blocks.prompt: A data set has standard deviation $1.75$. Find its variance, to 3 s.f.
Bakery P's loaves have mean mass $802$ g and standard deviation $4.1$ g. Bakery Q's have mean $806$ g and standard deviation $9.6$ g. Which statement is correct?
blocks.hint: A smaller standard deviation means the masses are less spread out.

options.text: Bakery P's loaves are heavier on average and more consistent
Bakery Q's loaves are heavier on average and more consistent
Bakery Q's loaves are heavier on average, but Bakery P's are more consistent

blocks.explain: Q's higher mean means heavier loaves on average. P's smaller standard deviation means its masses vary less.

verify.truth: Bakery Q's loaves are heavier on average, but Bakery P's are more consistent

sections.heading: Adding to or scaling every value

blocks.text: Add $3$ to every value. The [[mean|mean]] moves up by $3$, but the gaps between values don't change, so neither does the [[standard-deviation|standard deviation]].
Double every value instead. Every value and every gap doubles, so the mean and standard deviation both double.

blocks.alt: Three dot plots on one scale from 0 to 13. The original data 2, 3, 5 and 6 have mean 4. Adding 3 gives 5, 6, 8 and 9 with mean 7: the same pattern slid right. Doubling gives 4, 6, 10 and 12 with mean 8: the pattern stretched to twice the width.
blocks.caption: Adding $3$ slides the data, so only the mean changes. Doubling stretches it, so the mean and the spread both double.

blocks.statement: If every value $x$ becomes $ax + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants, the new mean is $a\bar{x} + b$ and the new standard deviation is $\lvert a\rvert\sigma$. The new variance is $a^{2}\sigma^{2}$.
blocks.why: Adding $b$ slides the data without changing any gap; multiplying by $a$ stretches every distance from the mean by $\lvert a\rvert$.

blocks.text: So subtracting $3$ from every value lowers the mean by $3$ and leaves $\sigma$ unchanged. The median changes like the mean, and so do the quartiles when $a > 0$; the IQR and range change like $\sigma$.

blocks.question: In a tournament, a golfer's round scores have mean $76.4$ strokes and standard deviation $3.8$ strokes. Each score is rewritten relative to par by subtracting $72$. Find the mean and the standard deviation of the new scores.
steps: Every score has $72$ subtracted: $x \to x - 72$.
Mean: $76.4 - 72 = 4.4$, so the golfer averages $4.4$ strokes over par.
Standard deviation: subtracting a constant doesn't change any gap, so $\sigma$ stays $3.8$.

blocks.question: An online shop's jackets have mean price €$128.50$ and standard deviation €$20.50$. For US buyers, each price is multiplied by $1.08$ to convert it to dollars, then a \$$15$ delivery charge is added. Find the mean and the standard deviation of the US prices.
steps: Each price $x$ becomes $1.08x + 15$.
Standard deviation: the $+15$ has no effect, so $\sigma = 1.08 \times 20.50 = 22.14$ dollars.
Adding $15$ to $\sigma$ too would give $37.14$, which is wrong.

blocks.text: Adding the constant to the standard deviation too. Adding or subtracting shifts the data and leaves $\sigma$ unchanged; only the multiplier affects it.

blocks.prompt: A data set has standard deviation $3.5$. Every value is doubled. Find the new standard deviation.
blocks.hint: Doubling every value doubles every distance from the mean.

blocks.prompt: A shop sells batteries in packs of $3$. The number of packs it sells each day has variance $1.44$. Find the variance of the number of batteries it sells each day.
blocks.hint: Each day's number of batteries is $3$ times its number of packs. Find the standard deviation first, then multiply it by $3$.
blocks.explain: $\sigma$ goes from $1.2$ packs to $3.6$ batteries, so the variance goes from $1.44$ to $3.6^{2} = 12.96$: it is multiplied by $3^{2}$.

blocks.prompt: A gym's scale read $0.4$ kg too heavy for every member. The recorded masses have mean $71.3$ kg and standard deviation $8.2$ kg. What are the correct mean and standard deviation?
blocks.hint: Every recorded mass must have $0.4$ subtracted.
blocks.explain: Subtracting $0.4$ lowers the mean to $70.9$ kg. It shifts every mass equally, so the standard deviation stays $8.2$ kg.

blocks.text: Median: the $\frac{n+1}{2}$th value in order; for even $n$, the mean of the middle two. Mode: the most frequent value.
Grouped data: estimate the mean with mid-interval values $\frac{a+b}{2}$. With equal class widths, the modal class is the class with the highest frequency.
Quartiles of discrete data: use the GDC. Methods differ, so a by-hand value can differ from the GDC's.
Standard deviation of a data set: GDC only, using $\sigma_{x}$, not $s_{x}$. Variance $= \sigma^{2}$: square the unrounded value.
Every value $x \to ax + b$: mean $\to a\bar{x} + b$, standard deviation $\to \lvert a\rvert\sigma$, variance $\to a^{2}\sigma^{2}$. Adding a constant leaves $\sigma$ unchanged.

mistakes: Quoting $s_{x}$ from the GDC as the standard deviation of a data set. Use $\sigma_{x}$, which divides by $n$.
Dividing $\sum f_{i}x_{i}$ by the number of columns or classes. Divide by the total frequency $n$.
Leaving the frequency list off on the GDC. Check that it shows the total frequency as $n$.
Adding the constant to the standard deviation. Under $x \to ax + b$, $\sigma$ becomes $\lvert a\rvert\sigma$; the $b$ has no effect.
Squaring a rounded standard deviation to get the variance. Square the GDC's full value.
Interpreting a standard deviation without mentioning spread. Say how spread out or consistent the values are, in context.
examTips: Write down the mode or modal class: no working needed. For Find the mean, show $\frac{\sum f_{i}x_{i}}{n}$ with numbers in, or your GDC lists, for the method mark.
Interpret a standard deviation by comparing spread in context, such as less variation in waiting times. Comparing averages alone earns no mark.
Explain why a grouped mean is an estimate: the actual values in each class are unknown, so mid-interval values stand in for them.
